extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers / worldbuilders (especially fantasy authors, including middle-grade writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for authors on creating and using magic systems in fiction — contrasting 'hard' (rule-based) and 'soft' (free-form) systems, with advice on sources, audience, narrative function, and how magic shapes plot and society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard vs soft magic distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Hard = rules, crunchy; Soft = more free-form, less explicit description of rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether your story needs a well-defined rule set or a looser, mysterious magic. Hard systems let you set up puzzles and causal expectations; soft systems create wonder and mystery. The hosts note younger readers often tolerate or prefer softer systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mythological/folkloric inspiration
rubrics_metrics.description: Draw on mythology or folklore (e.g., Shiva's third eye, Ganesh's mouse) as source material for magical ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can borrow elements directly and then 'change or craft it to fit' your story — adapt motifs to suit character, tone, and audience (example: The Third Eye borrows Shiva's third eye but makes it a hypnotic evil power). Use familiar myths to give resonance while tailoring mechanics to your narrative needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience considerations and tailoring complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Match the system's explicitness and complexity to your intended readers (middle-grade vs adult) and genre expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Middle-grade can get away with softer, less-explained magic; adult or puzzle-oriented novels may demand harder, crisper rules. Consider what readers want from the genre (escape, wish-fulfillment, social speculation) and tune complexity accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wish-fulfillment / escapism factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Magic often functions as aspirational 'geewhiz' or wish-fulfillment — readers want magic that feels fun and desirable (e.g., wanting to go to Hogwarts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage the aspirational aspect to hook readers, but balance it with other narrative needs. Not every system must be grim or costly; allowing moments of wonder increases reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magic-as-puzzle / set-up-and-payoff (plot coupons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design rule-based systems so the story becomes a puzzle: present the pieces and let readers (or characters) work out solutions; collect 'plot coupons' that are redeemed later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hard systems like Mistborn work as giant puzzles — set clear abilities/limitations so the climax's solutions feel earned. Use established mechanics to foreshadow and enable the finale without cheating the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual and sensory grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Give magic a visual/sensory component so readers can picture and emotionally experience it (example: Mistborn's 'blue lines').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if abilities are mental or abstract, adding visual/sensory markers helps readers understand what's happening and what it would feel like to use the power. This strengthens immersion and clarifies action scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprising, yet inevitable effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Strive for moments that are surprising but feel inevitable given the rules and setup (e.g., necromancy payoff in Deadbeat; Runelords' social consequences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When magic produces shocking outcomes, ensure they are logically consistent with established rules so the surprise satisfies rather than frustrates. The best payoffs provoke both 'Oh, wow' and 'Of course'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits, costs, and ramifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Define costs, limits, or trade-offs for magic to prevent it from being a narrative panacea and to create stakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make costs meaningful and explore their consequences (Runelords: branded strength creates dependency and social consequences). Costs can be personal, societal, or material, and should influence plot and character decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show societal and character-level consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider how magic reshapes institutions, relationships, and everyday life — not just individual fights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use magic to illuminate social themes (e.g., power imbalance, corruption). Demonstrate how societies adapt and how characters' roles change under different magical rules (Steelheart mapping of absolute power).

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal consistency and follow-through
rubrics_metrics.description: Once you establish rules or tendencies, follow through; deal with implications rather than ignoring them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should 'follow through on the ramifications' — address logical consequences of abilities and avoid deus ex machina. Consistency builds trust and allows you to craft satisfying resolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety and appropriateness of approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every magic system must follow the same design goals — some should be puzzle-like, some atmospheric; choose the approach that fits story tone and objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hosts emphasize variety: while they like puzzle-style systems, they value soft, atmospheric systems too (e.g., The Dark Is Rising, Prydain Chronicles). Be deliberate about which mode serves your narrative best.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimentation: hardening soft magic
rubrics_metrics.description: Try converting a soft magic system into a hard one (homework: 'Give Gandalf rules') to see how explicating rules changes story dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hardening a soft system is an exercise: it can reveal plot opportunities, change character agency, or expose hidden implications. Use this experiment to learn which level of explicitness best serves theme, tension, and reader satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character stakes and reliance on magic
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the magic system to create meaningful character dilemmas — removing support systems or making characters rely on (or against) magic can drive growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative choices like stripping away support (example: Tara losing her support system) force characters to confront magic's limits and their own resourcefulness, increasing emotional stakes and development.
